The Book Dossier — Building Our Own Table · November 2026

The FBACoin Receipts

Why does Black America need its own economic infrastructure? Not a slogan — a file. This dossier is the public, web-length version of the case Tooo Much lays out in his book Building Our Own Table: FBACoin and the Fight for the Next Generation: the harm, with receipts; the leak, with numbers; and the instrument built to answer both — the whitepaper in plain English, the locked treasury, the planned DAO, and the political argument. Every claim below carries the book’s labels: FACT (documented), BUILT (exists now, check it), PLANNED (a blueprint, not a product). Mae reads documents. Here is the document trail.

Status — The Book DossierThis dossier accompanies the book Building Our Own Table by Tooo Much. It is educational — history, economics, and an argument — not financial advice, and nothing on this page promises any return, profit, or price to anybody. Two separations the book keeps clean, kept clean here: FBACoin is not the reparations claim — the debt owed to Foundational Black Americans is older than any token and is not settled or traded away by this project. And token ownership is not proof of lineage — lineage is blood and record; it is not bought. The funnel, same as the book’s: start at fbacoin.org, read the whitepaper, then join the Telegram community linked there.

1. The Receipts — What Was Done

FACT Two hundred forty-six years of unpaid labor built the foundation, and the one material promise made at emancipation — Special Field Order No. 15, the “forty acres” — was revoked within the year; the land went back to the former enslavers. Reconstruction got twelve years. Then the taking changed instruments, era by era:

  • Terror as economic policy: Seneca Village, a Black landowning community, seized for Central Park; Wilmington 1898, a coup that burned a Black newspaper and overthrew a government; Greenwood, Tulsa, 1921 — 35 blocks of Black business wealth burned in two days (the official count said 39 dead; Oklahoma’s own 2001 commission said the toll may run as high as ~300 — both numbers stay on the receipt, flagged as they are in the book); Rosewood, 1923, a town erased.
  • Locked out by law: Black Codes, convict leasing, Jim Crow — then redlining: federal maps graded Black neighborhoods “hazardous” and the FHA refused to insure mortgages there for a generation while insuring the suburbs. The Census Bureau put Black homeownership at 45.9% against 73.8% for non-Hispanic white households in late 2023 — a gap wider than in 1970.
  • The modern takings: COINTELPRO, the crack era and mass incarceration, the 2008 foreclosure crisis’s reverse redlining, eminent domain and gentrification. The instrument changes. The direction doesn’t.

2. The Leak — Where the Money Goes Now

FACT Buying power is a river; wealth is a reservoir. The Selig Center estimates Black buying power at roughly $1.8 trillion a year (an estimate of flow, not a stock of wealth) — running through a community whose typical family holds $44,900 against a typical white family’s $285,000 (Federal Reserve, 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances). Census and Brookings figures put the ownership side at roughly 14.4% of the population, ~3% of employer firms, ~1% of business receipts. The money flows through our hands into economies we do not own.

One honesty note, because this site keeps its labels: the popular claim that the Black dollar “circulates for only six hours” is unsourced — a Howard University fact-check looked for it and it is not there. The book refuses to use it, and so does this page. The documented numbers are damning enough.

And the political twin of the leak is dilution: remedies widened until our share thins to nothing. California’s reparations task force held eligibility to lineage by a single 5–4 vote (March 29, 2022); the Fearless Fund was sued into retreat; the Supreme Court’s SFFA decision ended race-conscious admissions. Lineage is not a technicality. Lineage is the address on the debt.

Hear Mae — Section 2 — The Leak

3. What FBACoin Is — The Whitepaper in Plain English

FACT BUILT The source document is the FBACoin Whitepaper v1.3 (July 2026), free at fbacoin.org. The token, FBAC: a fixed supply of 1,000,000,000 — no mint function exists, so no more can ever be created — on Arbitrum One, trading on SushiSwap V2. Every buy and sell carries a 10% transaction tax, and 10% is the hard-coded maximum; it cannot be raised.

The tax splits six ways (§4.2): reflections 30% (shared pro rata among wallets holding at least 0.05% of supply, holder-claimed), loyalty 10% (wallets untouched for 7 consecutive days — any activity resets the clock), liquidity 20%, marketing 20%, burn 10%, and Whale Rewards 10% (§4.3 — a dividend pool for loyalty-eligible wallets holding at least 1% of supply). Mae prints the correction the book prints: this project’s own early summaries listed only five buckets and summed to 90%. The whitepaper had six all along. The document outranks the summary.

BUILT Utility, live today: FBAPay (fbapay.dev), a non-custodial payment processor — it never takes custody of your money. Its 1.5% merchant fee splits 50% to the treasury, 25% to a rewards vault, 15% to the development fund, 10% to liquidity (§7.1).

Hear Mae — Section 3 — What FBACoin Is

4. The Treasury — 651 Million, Locked

FACT BUILT The treasury holds 651,042,221 FBAC — 65.1% of supply — consolidated from the 300M genesis allocation, the Founder NFT program remainder, and a second-liquidity-seeding reserve, and locked in an immutable vault under a hard 180-day time-lock until December 29, 2026 (§3.1, §5). Not even the deployer can withdraw before expiry; reflections accruing in the vault sweep back to the treasury at unlock. Verify it on-chain yourself — the book’s Chapter 16 walks the check step by step.

PLANNED What it is for (§6): micro-loans, grants, scholarships, lobbying, emergency relief, marketing. Only two percentages are published — micro-loans 25% and marketing 5% of the treasury. The other four are named and pending DAO ratification; this page will not invent numbers the document hasn’t set. And the founder’s November 2026 policy, published to the community: no more large gifted allocations sitting loose in a single wallet — future promoter and team allocations are time-locked with scheduled releases. Rules before money moves.

Hear Mae — Section 4 — The Treasury

5. The DAO & the Think Tank — Planned, Not Live

PLANNED Say it first, the way the book does: the DAO is not live. Whitepaper §8 names the governance bodies — the Legacy Council, the Foundational 7, the Advisory Council, a Think Tank of roughly 12–14 members “focused on research and problem-solving,” a Compliance Department, and a voting body of token holders — and states in its own words that final voting weights and bylaws are pending ratification. Earlier weighting models are historical and not in force. The near-term priorities are printed in the document: ratify the bylaws, formalize treasury bucket governance, stand up lineage verification, open a public claim portal, fill open seats — lineage-verified members first.

The design is organized around five pillars (§1, §8) — economics, politics, education, media, justice — and the whitepaper names its own intellectual lineage: “The mission draws on the PowerNomics tradition of group economics and institution-building” (§2), Dr. Claud Anderson’s framework wired into on-chain infrastructure. Status by pillar, honestly: economics — BUILT (the token, FBAPay, the lock); media — partly BUILT (the tax routes 20% of every tax to marketing today, by code; the receipts function — dossiers like this one — is the working prototype); politics, education, justice — PLANNED (a lobbying line, a scholarship program, and a Compliance Department named in the drawing, awaiting ratification and staffing). The think tank’s function — research before positions, receipts before claims — is the one Mae performs on this site every week. The institution is planned. The habit is built.

Hear Mae — Section 5 — The DAO & the Think Tank

6. No Loyalty But Our Own

ARGUMENT The book’s political thesis, in the author’s own words:

“Black Americans should not be loyal to any political party but our own, because none of them represent us. Both parties ask us to deny who we are and what we stand for as a people and a lineage, and they want us to adopt their ideology and their agenda — which never addresses Black American issues. Our agenda is not theirs, and their agenda is not ours.” — Tooo Much

The exhibits, condensed (the book’s Chapters 24–25 carry the full record):

  • The Democratic record: 200+ anti-lynching bills blocked across the decades — the Dyer bill filibustered in the Senate — and no federal anti-lynching law until 2022. The 1994 Crime Bill and 1996 welfare law signed by a Democratic president. Executive action that moved for other constituencies — DACA, TPS, humanitarian parole — while H.R. 40, the reparations study bill introduced in every Congress since 1989, has never received a floor vote (its high-water mark: a 25–17 committee markup, April 14, 2021). Juneteenth’s federal holiday passed 415–14. Symbolism moves unanimous. Substance never reaches the floor.
  • The Republican record: the honest beginning first — founded 1854, emancipation and the Reconstruction amendments are real. Then Goldwater’s 1964 vote against the Civil Rights Act, Thurmond’s party switch the same year, Kevin Phillips describing the strategy in 1969, Lee Atwater’s 1981 interview (the verified quote only — this site checks its quotes), and RNC Chairman Ken Mehlman’s 2005 apology to the NAACP for the strategy by name. Crack-to-powder sentencing at 100-to-1 for a generation, softened only to 18-to-1 in 2010. Shelby County v. Holder (2013) gutted Voting Rights Act preclearance; North Carolina’s legislature answered with a law the Fourth Circuit struck down for targeting Black voters with “almost surgical precision.”

ARGUMENT The book’s answer (Chapter 26): an independent FBA party — local first, a lineage agenda, candidates vetted against it, party funds kept separate from the Treasury and the DAO. And the answer to the spoiler charge, in the book’s words: a vote owed to no one cannot be taken from anyone.

Hear Mae — Section 6 — No Loyalty But Our Own

7. What You Do Monday Morning

  1. Read the whitepaper yourself — free at fbacoin.org. Don’t let anybody, Mae included, be your only source on a document you can read.
  2. Join the community through the front door — the Telegram link at fbacoin.org, and only there.
  3. Learn the wallet safety rules before any money moves: no admin will ever DM you first; nobody will ever ask for your seed phrase — anyone who does is a thief; write it on paper, keep it offline; impostor tokens exist, so the only route to the real one is through fbacoin.org. Learn first. Your pace, your research, your decision.
  4. First-look habit: this week, before the big platform gets your money, look for the Black-owned business first.
  5. Teach one family member one receipt from this page.
  6. Write down your lineage — names, places, records. A written lineage is protection against the quiet losses (heirs’ property is the book’s example) and the foundation the claim stands on. Protect the lineage, protect the future.

Mae’s VerdictThe harm is documented. The leak is measured. The instrument is built to be checked — a fixed supply, a six-bucket tax printed in its own whitepaper, a treasury locked in public until a date anybody can verify, a governor drawn and honestly labeled planned, and a politics that answers to the lineage first. That is the whole case, and it fits on one page because the receipts carry it. Start where the book starts: fbacoin.org → the whitepaper → the Telegram community. Then check everything Mae just told you. That was always the deal.

The Sources

This dossier condenses Building Our Own Table (Tooo Much, 2026), whose Appendix A indexes 165 distinct sources across 27 chapters. The load-bearing ones for this page:

  • FBACoin, Whitepaper v1.3 (July 2026) — §1–§2 (mission, five pillars, PowerNomics lineage), §3.1 & §5 (supply, treasury lock), §4.2–§4.3 (the six-bucket tax, Whale Rewards), §6 (treasury programs), §7.1 (FBAPay), §8 (governance, pending ratification). Read it at fbacoin.org.
  • Federal Reserve, 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances — typical family wealth, $285,000 / $44,900.
  • U.S. Census Bureau — Housing Vacancies and Homeownership (Q4 2023) and the Annual Business Survey; Brookings Institution analyses of Black business ownership; Selig Center for Economic Growth — Black buying power estimate (~$1.8T, a flow estimate).
  • Oklahoma Commission to Study the Tulsa Race Riot of 1921 (2001) — the confirmed toll and the higher estimate, both printed.
  • California Reparations Task Force (AB 3121) — the March 29, 2022 lineage-eligibility vote, 5–4.
  • U.S. House Judiciary Committee — H.R. 40 markup, April 14, 2021 (25–17); the bill’s introduction record since 1989; Juneteenth National Independence Day Act vote, 415–14.
  • Shelby County v. Holder, 570 U.S. 529 (2013); N.C. State Conference of the NAACP v. McCrory, 831 F.3d 204 (4th Cir. 2016) — “almost surgical precision”; Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, 600 U.S. 181 (2023); Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 (100-to-1 → 18-to-1).
  • Dr. Claud Anderson, PowerNomics: The National Plan to Empower Black America (2001) — the framework the whitepaper cites.
